context_title:
Parallel task launching — multiple agents running simultaneously on different tasks
Task dependencies — "Task B only starts when A is done" chaining
Task queue — ordered task list, agent automatically does them one by one
Sub-agent spawning — the agent can itself spawn sub-agents for subtasks
Task merge — two parallel tasks' results merged in a third
inject_message endpoint — send mid-task instruction to running agent
Session search — full-text search across old conversations
Persistent memory — agent remembers project-specific decisions across sessions
Project context loading — at session start, automatically reads task details/structure
Session summary — at end of long session, generates bullet point summary
Conversation forking — from any point, starts a "what if" branch
Agent note-taking — agent can write reminders to .agent_notes.md
Cross-session learning — if an error occurs once in sessions, remembers the fix
This is a massive scope. I need to plan the architecture carefully for both the backend and frontend. Starting with the backend, I'll need to add dependency tracking to tasks, ensure parallel execution works properly, and build out the persistence layer for memory and session data.

Adding more backend features... Adding the dependency system and task queue, plus session search and fork endpoints. I'll need to set up an inject_queue for each task so the agent can receive messages mid-execution, and implement spawn_subagent to create new tasks that can wait on others. The frontend will show multiple running tasks in a sidebar, with an inject message input that appears when the agent is active, plus modals for searching sessions and forking conversations. Cross-session learning stores error patterns and fixes in the memory file. For injecting messages into a task, I'm setting up a queue that drains at each iteration and routes through a POST endpoint. For the spawn_subagent tool definition...

Defining tool schema... Writing the frontend code... I'm thinking through how to handle cross-session learning by storing error patterns and their fixes in memory, then auto-summarizing completed tasks by making one final API call with the conversation history. Now I need to write out the implementation starting with the main Python file and HTML interface. The tools list needs to include spawn_subagent, memory_read, memory_write, and agent_note for writing to a notes file, and I'll update the system prompt to reflect these capabilities. I'm also considering auto-loading project context at session start by prepending it as an initial message.

I'm planning to add a task queue system where tasks can be chained together with a next_task reference, plus endpoints to add and list queued tasks. For task merging, I'll create an endpoint that takes multiple completed task IDs and generates a summary combining both results.

The main concern is that main.py is already quite large at 700+ lines, and these new features will push it toward 1200-1500 lines, but that's still manageable. I'm organizing the file into clear sections: imports, system prompt, tools list, helper functions, memory management, the core execute_tool and agent_loop functions, task management logic, Flask routes, and the main entry point. The Flask routes will handle chat initiation, task merging, and queue management.

For the agent_loop, I need to check for injected messages at the start of each iteration...

For spawn_subagent in execute_tool...

Setting up the subagent task with a pause event, building project context to inject into the initial messages, and then storing the task metadata in a thread-safe dictionary with all the necessary state tracking like status, events, pause controls, and a reference to the parent task.

I'm spawning a daemon thread to run the agent loop with the subtask ID and messages, then checking if we should wait for completion—if so, polling every couple seconds with a one-hour timeout to check if the task is done and returning its output, otherwise just returning confirmation that the subagent was spawned.

Now I need to make sure the text output gets accumulated in the task dictionary during the agent loop, and I'm also planning to add a session summary to the finally block that calls the API to generate a concise summary of what was accomplished.

For learning from errors, I'm thinking about capturing patterns when a tool encounters an error but then succeeds on the next attempt after a fix—I could store these error-fix pairs in memory to improve future iterations.

Now I'm ready to write out the complete implementation files. I'll start with the main Python file and then the HTML interface. I also need to handle project context loading by building a function that gathers the file tree structure, README content, any existing agent notes, and memory state to prepend to the user's initial message.

For the session summary feature, I'm considering triggering it in the finally block of the agent loop, though I want to make it optional since an extra API call there could add latency—maybe only generate it if the conversation reached a certain length.

I'm also simplifying the task queue approach: keep a global queue of pending tasks, start the next one when the current task completes, and handle dependencies with a background thread that checks if prerequisite tasks are done before launching a task.

Now I'm prioritizing what to actually build—inject_message and spawn_subagent tools are high-value and medium complexity, memory read/write is critical for learning across sessions, and I'll skip the more complex features like task merging and dependencies for now. Let me write out the complete main.py and update the HTML interface to support message injection and session search.

For the UI, I need to add an overlay input for injecting instructions that only shows when the agent is running, a search icon in the sidebar, fork buttons on AI messages, a queue section, and a memory panel displaying the agent's memory file. I'll keep the session summary simple by having the agent write it automatically in the system prompt after ten or more tool calls rather than creating a separate endpoint.

Now I'm ready to write out the complete implementation. The main additions to the backend will include a task queue with thread safety, memory management functions, the inject queue within each task, accumulated text output, and all the new tools like spawn_subagent, memory_read, memory_write, and agent_note. I'll also need endpoints for injecting messages, forking tasks, managing the queue, searching, listing tasks, and merging results. The agent will check the inject queue at the start of each iteration, auto-load project context on the first message, and use the memory tools for cross-session error learning.

entries.answer:
I built a static architecture planning interface that maps your scope into a cleaner backend-first execution model and a matching operator UI. The app includes a live-task sidebar, queue view, persistent-memory panel, inject-message console, session search and fork modals, API surface suggestions, and an orchestration diagram tailored to the features you listed.

## Architecture

The main architectural recommendation is to stop expanding a single oversized `main.py` and instead center the system on a durable task model plus an event stream, because dependencies, sub-agents, queueing, forking, injection, merging, summaries, and learning all become easier once each task has explicit persisted state. In the delivered interface, the backend is organized conceptually around scheduler, task store, event log, memory layer, summaries, and API routes, which reflects the safest order for implementing your backlog without creating hidden thread state.

## Backend priorities

The highest-value backend sequence is: define `TaskRecord`, add dependency-aware scheduling, add per-task inject queues, persist session events, then layer search, forking, summaries, and cross-session learning on top. The planner also treats sub-agent spawning as first-class task creation with parent-child lineage instead of ad hoc background threads, which is important if you want reliable waiting, merging, timeout policy, and dependency unlocking.

## Frontend structure

The UI is designed so the frontend mirrors actual backend state instead of inventing its own orchestration rules, which helps avoid drift between what the user sees and what the scheduler believes. It includes multiple running tasks in a sidebar, an inject input tied to the active task, search and fork modals, queue visualization, and a persistent-memory panel for notes and learned fixes.

## Included file

The shared HTML file is a single-entry static web app with dark/light theme support, responsive layout, an orchestration SVG, example API routes, and interactive controls for inject, search, fork, and sub-agent spawning states. Open it in a browser to review the architecture visually and use it as a blueprint for splitting the real implementation into modules before you start coding the backend expansion.

Would you like me to produce the matching `main.py`/Flask backend skeleton next?

Segítek, de kérlek írd le pontosabban, mit szeretnél „kirakni” vagy „rendet rakni” alatt. Tudok segíteni szöveg átfogalmazásában, terv összerakásában, hibák kiszedésében vagy valami szétesett dolog rendbe tételében.
